paragraphs.text: Immunodeficiency-35 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by TYK2 deficiency. The first reported patient was clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) (Minegishi et al., 2006). Kreins et al. (2015) studied 8 patients from 6 families. They concluded that the core clinical phenotype of autosomal recessive complete TYK2 deficiency is mycobacterial and/or viral infections caused by impaired responses to IL-12 and IFN-alpha/beta. They also concluded that impaired IL-6 responses and HIES do not appear to be intrinsic features of TYK2 deficiency in humans.

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy born to first-cousin parents. After BCG vaccination at 2 months of age, he developed disseminated BCG disease. Left axillary lymphadenopathy appeared at 8 months. By 21 months he had generalized fistulous cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymphadenopathy with fever. M. bovis BCG was isolated from discharging sinuses, and lymph node histology showed acid-fast bacilli. He recovered without relapse after 18 months of antimycobacterial therapy. At age 8 years he developed neurobrucellosis, with seizures, neck stiffness, and Brucella-positive blood and CSF cultures. This left him with severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, and lacunar infarcts on MRI. At 11 years he had herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which was treated with acyclovir and did not recur.

paragraphs.text: Unlike the first reported Japanese TYK2-deficient patient, the patient of Kilic et al. (2012) had no features of HIES. He had no atopy, asthma, eczema, staphylococcal or candidal skin infections, and no skeletal or dental abnormalities. His serum IgE ranged from 80 to 218 IU/ml, which was normal or only slightly elevated. Serum IgG, IgM, and IgA levels, lymphocyte subsets, and the NBT test were normal. The authors suggested that TYK2 deficiency should be considered in patients with BCG disease or other intramacrophage infections, particularly those with severe herpesvirus infections, even in the absence of HIES features.

This contrasted with the previously reported Japanese patient (P1), who had atopic dermatitis, high IgE, and staphylococcal abscesses.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2022) studied an international cohort of 112 children under 16 years of age who were hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia. Twelve (10.7%) had recessive complete inborn errors of type I IFN immunity. These were X-linked recessive TLR7 deficiency (7 children) and autosomal recessive deficiency of IFNAR1 (1), STAT2 (1), or TYK2 (3). None of these 15 recessive deficiencies was found in 1,224 SARS-CoV-2-infected controls without pneumonia (P = 1.2 x 10(-11)). The 3 TYK2-deficient children (P2-P4) were unrelated and consanguineous Turkish. Whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing found that all 3 were homozygous for the same TYK2 frameshift variant, P216Rfs*14, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Family segregation analysis confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance, and the authors confirmed that the variant was loss-of-function. Eight of the 12 patients in the series were tested for autoantibodies against type I IFNs, and all were negative. The authors identified autosomal recessive TYK2 deficiency as a new genetic cause of COVID-19 pneumonia.

The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression in patient cells, and the authors confirmed that it was loss-of-function.
